content.intro: This lesson focuses on version control for structured documents and connects the PDF syllabus topics to a small, inspectable example. Work from the intended data model, write down the expected result, then verify syntax and semantics with the target tool.
content.why_it_matters: Version Control for Structured Documents matters because structured-data files sit between people, tools, services, and deployment systems. A clear contract and repeatable checks make the result easier to maintain and safer to consume.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Reliable structured-data repositories use positive and negative tests, golden fixtures, contract tests, reviewed diffs, versioned schemas, CI checks, and production observability. Make checks repeatable so configuration mistakes fail before deployment.

content_blocks.title: What you will cover
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly addresses: Tracking JSON and YAML changes. Meaningful commit messages. Reviewing configuration diffs. Pull request validation.; Merge conflicts. Branching and release practices. Protecting secret-bearing files.. Treat each as part of a workflow: define what the data should mean, represent it consistently, and test how the chosen implementation interprets it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Version Control for Structured Documents
content_blocks.code:
Review a structured-data diff for:
- field additions/removals/type changes
- reordered arrays
- comments lost in conversion
- secret or environment-specific values
- changes to schema/tool versions
content_blocks.expected_output: Version control is most effective when diffs are reviewed for semantic and security impact, not only textual changes.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect the example and compare it against the lesson concepts. This code block is static-validation: CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary data parsers or commands in the standard browser preview.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the starting fixture before each test. Change one field, indentation level, parser option, or schema constraint at a time, then compare the result with the prediction.

items.title: 1. State the contract
items.text: Write down the expected root type, required fields, scalar types, and any compatibility assumptions.

items.title: 2. Validate before use
items.text: Parse the document and run the applicable schema or policy checks; syntax success alone is not full correctness.

items.title: 3. Test a boundary
items.text: Include at least one missing, malformed, ambiguous, or unexpected input and record the desired behavior.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Treat configuration as code: validate it before use, keep secrets out of the file, review changes, and test both the expected configuration and failure behavior. Confirm implementation-specific behavior against the target parser, tool version, and standards documentation.

Predict the parsed types/result, change one relevant detail, and record whether the target tool behaved as expected. Include one invalid or boundary case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating readable text as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Syntax and visual formatting cannot establish data types, schema conformance, or application-specific meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse, validate against the intended contract, and test a valid plus an invalid fixture.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming every parser interprets the feature identically.
common_mistakes.why: Format versions, schema choices, library defaults, and product-specific restrictions affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the exact parser/version and test the target environment.

common_mistakes.why: Missing fields, wrong types, duplicate keys, or ambiguous scalars may still break consumers.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep valid, invalid, and boundary fixtures in version control.
